semantic_correction.stem: An older adult takes twelve medications prescribed by several clinicians. Which concern should the nurse prioritize during medication review?

options.A: Reconcile prescriptions from every prescriber together with OTC medicines, vitamins, supplements, and herbals, and assess for interactions, duplicate therapy, adverse effects, ongoing need, and management difficulty.
options.B: Review prescriptions written for the current admission and defer products from other prescribers, OTC medicines, vitamins, and supplements to a later outpatient visit.
options.C: Rank the medications by how long the client has taken them and recommend discontinuing the oldest therapies first unless a new symptom or adverse effect appears.
options.D: Confirm that each medicine has a valid prescriber and continue the regimen unchanged, because individual prescriptions do not require a combined interaction review.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current National Institute on Aging guidance states that older adults often have multiple health conditions and take many medicines, increasing the risk of side effects and other unintended problems. NIA advises patients and clinicians to maintain and review a complete medication list that includes prescriptions from all prescribers, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, dietary supplements, and herbal remedies. The guidance specifically warns that mixing these products can be dangerous and that duplicate active ingredients and drug interactions can occur. NIA also recommends asking at visits whether every medicine is still needed and discussing whether any can be safely reduced or stopped. Therefore the priority is a comprehensive medication reconciliation and review of the whole regimen for interactions, duplication, adverse effects, ongoing need, and management burden. B is incorrect because excluding medicines from other prescribers or nonprescription products creates an incomplete review. C is incorrect because duration of therapy by itself is not an appropriate deprescribing criterion. D is incorrect because individually valid prescriptions can still interact, duplicate therapy, or create cumulative medication burden when combined.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Perform comprehensive medication review in older adults with polypharmacy by reconciling all prescription and nonprescription products and assessing interactions, duplication, adverse effects, ongoing need, and medication-management burden.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests comprehensive medication review in an older adult with polypharmacy with one clearly best answer, balanced alternatives, current NIA guidance, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It reflects NIA guidance to review the entire regimen across prescribers and nonprescription products for interactions, duplication, adverse effects, necessity, and management issues.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Deferring medicines from other prescribers and nonprescription products produces an incomplete medication reconciliation and can miss important interactions or duplication.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Medication age is not an evidence-based stand-alone criterion for deprescribing; ongoing indication, risk, benefit, adverse effects, and interactions are more relevant.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Multiple individually prescribed medicines can still interact, duplicate ingredients or effects, and create clinically important polypharmacy burden when taken together.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely performs complete cross-prescriber and nonprescription reconciliation plus clinical review; B is incomplete, C uses an arbitrary deprescribing rule, and D falsely assumes individually valid prescriptions are safe in combination.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel medication-review approaches of comparable length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct response was removed and no absolute-word pattern identifies the key.
